facts.statement: The name Pissarrachampsa means "sandstone crocodile" in reference to the local name of the sandstones where the fossils were found.
facts.quote: Pissarrachampsa (meaning "piçarra [the local name for the sandstones it was recovered from] crocodile") is an extinct genus of baurusuchid mesoeucrocodylian from the Late Cretaceous of Brazil.

facts.statement: Fossils of Pissarrachampsa were found near Gurinhatã, Brazil, in the Late Cretaceous Vale do Rio do Peixe Formation.
facts.quote: It is based on a nearly complete skull and a referred partial skull and lower jaw from the ?Campanian - ?Maastrichtian-age Vale do Rio do Peixe Formation of the Bauru Group, found in the vicinity of Gurinhatã, Brazil.

facts.statement: The genus Pissarrachampsa was described by Montefeltro, Larsson, and Langer in 2011.
The snout of Pissarrachampsa was relatively short, making up about 70% of the total skull length, which is shorter than in other crocodyliforms.
facts.quote: The snout is not as narrow as other related baurusuchids, however. At around 70% the length of the entire skull, the snout is also short in comparison to those of other crocodyliforms.

facts.statement: Pissarrachampsa likely had a reduced number of teeth in the groove behind the maxillary teeth compared to other baurusuchids.
facts.quote: Pissarrachampsa likely lost these teeth, giving it a reduced dentition.

facts.statement: A deep notch between the upper jaw bones allowed an enlarged fourth tooth in the lower jaw to fit when the mouth was closed.
facts.quote: A deep notch between the maxillae and premaxillae provides room for an enlarged fourth dentary tooth in the lower jaw when the mouth is closed.

facts.statement: Thick rims around the large triangular holes on the skull roof are a unique diagnostic feature of Pissarrachampsa.
facts.quote: The thick anterior and medial rims of the supratemporal fenestrae are a diagnostic feature of Pissarrachampsa.

facts.statement: Unlike other baurusuchids, the four small depressions at the back of the Pissarrachampsa skull are visible from the side view.
facts.quote: In Pissarrachampsa, these fenestrae are visible when the skull is viewed from the side, but in other baurusuchids, they are hidden within a deep notch in the back of the skull.

facts.statement: Pissarrachampsa had four Eustachian tube openings under the skull, with the outer pair being larger than the inner pair.
facts.quote: Another unique feature can be found underneath the back of the skull; four holes called Eustachian foramina provide an opening for the Eustachian tubes, and in Pissarrachampsa the outer or lateral pair are larger than the inner or medial pair.

facts.statement: Pissarrachampsa likely preyed on sauropods and other crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: Pissarrachampsa may have preyed upon sauropods (such as Adamantisaurus, Aeolosaurus, Gondwanatitan, Maxakalisaurus, and nemegtosaurids) and other crocodylomorphs (such as Caipirasuchus, Caryonosuchus, Sphagesaurus, Adamantinasuchus, Labidiosuchus, Mariliasuchus, Morrinhosuchus, and Barreirosuchus).

facts.statement: Pissarrachampsa was likely preyed upon by theropod dinosaurs including abelisaurids, carcharodontosaurids, and megaraptora.
facts.quote: And in turn, Pissarrachampsa may have been preyed upon by theropods (such as abelisaurids, carcharodontosaurids and megaraptora).

facts.statement: Pissarrachampsa likely laid small clutches of only 4 to 5 eggs and provided extensive parental care, a trait more common in modern mammals than crocodiles.
facts.quote: More unusually, Pissarrachampsa seems to have been a K-strategist breeder; as the nests contain only 4-5 eggs each, it is likely that it was more extensive in its parental care than modern crocodiles and invested more time and energy into raising its young.

facts.statement: A 2014 study confirmed that Pissarrachampsa belongs to the subfamily Pissarrachampsinae.
facts.quote: A recent study from 2014 corroborates with the original description and places Pissarrachampsa sera within the subfamily Pissarrachampsinae:

facts.statement: Pissarrachampsa lived between 83.6 and 66 million years ago during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Pissarrachampsa had a deep skull that was narrow in front of the eyes and wider at the back, creating a roughly triangular shape from above.
rejected.quote: Like other baurusuchids, it has a deep skull that narrow in front of the eyes and wider at the back, giving it a roughly triangular shape when viewed from above.
